Tips.Title: Run your monitor at its full refresh rate, from the graphics card
Tips.Body: A 144 Hz screen left at 60 Hz, or a cable in the motherboard instead of the graphics card, costs more than any tweak can win back.

Tips.Title: Turn on XMP or EXPO in the BIOS
Tips.Body: Without it, RAM runs at its slow fallback speed (DDR4 3,200, DDR5 4,800). It's one switch and one of the biggest free gains in CPU-heavy games.

Tips.Title: Enable Resizable BAR
Tips.Body: Lets the CPU reach all of the graphics card's memory at once. Usually a few percent, over 15% in some games. In the BIOS: CSM off, Above 4G Decoding on, Re-Size BAR on.

Tips.Title: Let shaders build, and stop wiping them
Tips.Body: New games compile shaders the first time an effect appears, causing hitches that fade. Let the pre-compile step finish, raise the driver's shader cache (10 GB or Unlimited), and skip cleaner apps that delete it.

Tips.Title: Use G-SYNC or FreeSync with the right frame cap
Tips.Body: Variable refresh on, V-Sync on in the driver and off in the game. With Reflex on, the driver caps for you (about 138 FPS at 144 Hz); without it, cap a few FPS under your refresh rate.

Tips.Title: Best performance power mode, Game Mode on, background recording off
Tips.Body: The Windows settings that still measurably help. On laptops, use Best performance only when plugged in.

Tips.Title: Games on an SSD, and watch the temperatures
Tips.Body: New games stutter badly on hard drives. Drops that start after 5 to 15 minutes usually mean heat: clean the dust, fix airflow, repaste or undervolt.

Tips.Title: Memory Integrity: test before turning it off
Tips.Body: Windows turned it on for many PCs with the October 2026 update. On modern CPUs it costs under 2% in 2026 tests; older CPUs lose more. Turning it off removes real protection, so only do it if you measure a difference.

Skip.Title: Registry cleaners
Skip.Body: No measurable effect on modern Windows, and a real chance of breaking installed software.

Skip.Title: Turning off the page file
Skip.Body: Games and Windows expect one. Without it you get crashes when memory runs out, not speed.

Skip.Title: Old "FPS boost" registry packs
Skip.Body: Many 2017-era tweaks no longer do anything on Windows 11 24H2 and later.

Skip.Title: Forcing MSI mode on every device
Skip.Body: Modern graphics and network drivers already use it. Forcing it on devices that don't support it can stop Windows from starting.

Skip.Title: Turning off fullscreen optimizations
Skip.Body: On Windows 10 and 11 they give fullscreen speed with fast alt-tab. Only try it for one old game that misbehaves.

Skip.Title: RAM cleaners and 'game booster' apps
Skip.Body: Emptying memory just makes Windows load it again. Free RAM isn't faster RAM.

Skip.Title: Changing DNS for lower ping
Skip.Body: DNS only finds the server's address before you connect. In-game ping doesn't change.

Skip.Title: Timer resolution tools
Skip.Body: Windows 11 already gives games the timer they ask for, and forcing it for everything raises power use.

Guides.Title: NVIDIA settings for smooth, low-latency games
Guides.Summary: The NVIDIA App and Control Panel settings that actually matter, and the G-SYNC recipe Blur Busters measured as best.

Steps.Text: Plug the monitor into the graphics card, not the motherboard.
NVIDIA Control Panel → Change resolution: pick your monitor's highest refresh rate (144 Hz, 165 Hz, 240 Hz...). Windows often leaves it at 60.
On the same page, set Output dynamic range to Full. Over HDMI it's often Limited, which makes blacks look grey.
Install drivers from the NVIDIA App or nvidia.com. Update when a game you play needs it or a fix you want is listed; you don't need every release.

Chapters.Title: The G-SYNC recipe
Chapters.Intro: Blur Busters' tested settings for no tearing with the least input lag. They also work for 'G-SYNC Compatible' FreeSync monitors.

Steps.Text: Set up G-SYNC: turn it on (for fullscreen, or fullscreen and windowed if you play borderless).
Manage 3D settings → Vertical sync: On. Then turn V-Sync off in every game.
Cap FPS at least 3 below your refresh rate: 141 at 144 Hz, 162 at 165 Hz, 237 at 240 Hz. Use the game's limiter first, otherwise 'Max Frame Rate' in the Control Panel.
Games with NVIDIA Reflex: turn Reflex on. With G-SYNC and V-Sync on, it caps for you (about 138 FPS at 144 Hz), so you can skip your own cap there.
Games without Reflex: set Low Latency Mode to On. 'Ultra' also caps automatically with G-SYNC.
Shader Cache Size: 10 GB or Unlimited, so games don't recompile shaders (and hitch) as often.
NVIDIA App → Graphics → DLSS Override: set the model preset to Latest, so older games use the newest DLSS.
Power management mode: leave it on Normal. Use 'Prefer maximum performance' for one game only if its clocks drop and it stutters; it raises idle power.
Leave the rest at default. Texture filtering, anisotropic and the like make no measurable FPS difference on a modern card.

Guides.Title: AMD Software settings for smooth, low-latency games
Guides.Summary: FreeSync, Anti-Lag, frame caps and what to leave off in AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition.

Steps.Text: Plug the monitor into the graphics card, and set its highest refresh rate in Windows → Settings → Display → Advanced display.
AMD Software → Settings → Display: turn on AMD FreeSync for your monitor.
Turn Enhanced Sync off; it can cause stutter with FreeSync.
Use the Default graphics profile, not HYPR-RX: HYPR-RX switches on several features at once, including ones that lower resolution or add generated frames.
AMD Anti-Lag: on. In games that support Anti-Lag 2, turn it on in the game's own settings.
Wait for Vertical Refresh: 'Always on' if you want no tearing with FreeSync, then turn V-Sync off in the game.
Cap FPS 3 below your refresh rate with the game's limiter, or with Radeon Chill set to the same minimum and maximum.
Radeon Boost: off for competitive games. It lowers the resolution while you move.
Get drivers from AMD Software or amd.com. If a game stutters after an update, try the shader cache reset in Graphics → Advanced once.
To undervolt a Radeon card, use AMD Software: Performance → Tuning → Custom, then lower the maximum voltage in small steps and test each one in your game.

Guides.Title: BIOS: XMP/EXPO and Resizable BAR
Guides.Summary: The two BIOS switches most gaming PCs are missing, with the menu names for ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte and ASRock boards.

Steps.Text: Restart and press Delete (or F2) repeatedly as the PC starts. Or in Windows: Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced startup → Restart now → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → UEFI Firmware Settings.
Most boards open in an Easy mode. Press F7 to switch to Advanced mode if you can't find a setting.

Chapters.Title: Turn on XMP or EXPO
Chapters.Intro: Without it, RAM runs at its slow fallback speed (DDR4 2,133 to 3,200, DDR5 4,800). It's one of the biggest free gains in CPU-heavy games.

Steps.Text: ASUS: Ai Tweaker → Ai Overclock Tuner → XMP I (or EXPO). MSI: the A-XMP or EXPO button on the main screen. Gigabyte: Tweaker → Extreme Memory Profile (X.M.P.). ASRock: OC Tweaker → DRAM Profile → XMP or EXPO.
Save and exit (usually F10). The first start can take a minute or two while the PC trains the memory, especially with DDR5. Don't turn it off.
Check it worked: Task Manager → Performance → Memory → Speed should show your kit's rated speed, for example 6000 MT/s.
Steps.Tip: Pulse's Diagnose page checks this too.

Steps.Text: Won't start, or crashes? Clear the CMOS (the button on the back, or the jumper in the manual) and try the second XMP profile or one speed step lower.

Chapters.Title: Turn on Resizable BAR
Chapters.Intro: Lets the CPU reach all of the graphics card's memory at once. Usually a few percent, more in some games. AMD calls it Smart Access Memory.

Steps.Text: Turn CSM (Compatibility Support Module) off. Windows 11 already boots without it.
Turn Above 4G Decoding on, then Re-Size BAR Support on (or Auto). It's usually under Advanced → PCI Subsystem Settings.
Check it: NVIDIA Control Panel → System Information → Resizable BAR: Yes. On AMD, AMD Software → Performance shows Smart Access Memory.
Update the BIOS only to fix a problem or support a new CPU, and only from your motherboard maker's support page for your exact model.
An update resets XMP/EXPO and Resizable BAR, so turn them back on afterwards.
Steps.Warn: Never turn the PC off during a BIOS update.

Guides.Title: Clean graphics driver reinstall with DDU
Guides.Summary: The fix for crashes, black screens and stutter that started after a driver update, or when switching between NVIDIA and AMD.

Steps.Text: Download the driver you want to install first (from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel) and keep it on the desktop.
Download Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) from its official site, Wagnardsoft, and unzip it.
In Pulse, turn on 'Stop Windows Update replacing your graphics driver' so Windows doesn't sneak its own driver in while you work.
Unplug the network cable or turn Wi-Fi off.
Restart into Safe Mode: hold Shift and click Restart → Troubleshoot → Advanced options → Startup Settings → Restart → press 4.
Run DDU, pick GPU and your brand on the right, then 'Clean and restart'.
Back in Windows, run the driver you downloaded. On NVIDIA pick Custom → Clean installation if offered.
Reconnect to the internet, then set your refresh rate and driver settings again (the NVIDIA or AMD settings guide).

Guides.Title: Fix stutter and FPS drops
Guides.Summary: Work out what kind of stutter you have, then fix the cause: shaders, video memory, background apps, storage, heat or frame pacing.

Chapters.Title: Find the kind of stutter
Chapters.Intro: Turn on Pulse's performance overlay (Games page) and watch its frame-time graph while it happens.

Steps.Text: Spikes the first time you see an effect or a new area, fewer the second time: shader compilation. See the next chapter.
Regular spikes every few seconds, even standing still: something in the background. See 'Background apps'.
FPS fine at first, then dropping after 10 to 20 minutes: heat. See the cooling guide.
Hitching in big or detailed areas, with video memory near full in the overlay: VRAM. Lower texture quality one step.
Pulse's Diagnose page checks the common causes for you: refresh rate, RAM speed, power plan, drivers and more.
Let the game's 'compiling shaders' step finish before you play, even if it takes minutes.
Raise the driver's shader cache to 10 GB or Unlimited (NVIDIA) and don't let cleaner apps wipe it. Pulse's cleanup never deletes it.
After a driver update, expect the first session in each game to hitch again while shaders rebuild.
Close what you don't need while playing: browser tabs with video, launchers you're not using, RGB and peripheral apps you don't need open.
Only one overlay and one recorder at a time (Discord, Steam, NVIDIA, Xbox Game Bar, Medal). Each one hooks into the game.
Pause big downloads and Windows Update while you play, or use Pulse's tweak that limits update bandwidth.
Trim what starts with Windows on Pulse's Startup apps page.
Games on an SSD, with at least 10 to 15% of the drive free.
RAM in two matching sticks (dual channel), with XMP or EXPO on. One stick halves memory bandwidth.
Laptops: plugged in, on the maker's performance mode, with the game running on the dedicated graphics card.
Cap your FPS a little below what you can hold most of the time. Steady 120 feels smoother than 120 to 200 jumping around.

Guides.Title: Lower ping and stop lag spikes
Guides.Summary: What actually lowers ping and stops spikes: the connection, Wi-Fi placement, bufferbloat and downloads. Plus the popular fixes that don't work.

Steps.Text: Use an Ethernet cable if you can. It removes most lag spikes Wi-Fi causes. Powerline adapters are the next best thing.
On Wi-Fi: connect on 5 GHz or 6 GHz, not 2.4 GHz, and keep the router in the open, not in a cupboard or behind the TV.
Pick the game server or region closest to you. Distance is most of your ping, and no PC setting changes it.

Chapters.Title: Bufferbloat: lag when someone else downloads

Steps.Text: Run Waveform's bufferbloat test. A grade of C or worse means your ping jumps whenever the connection is busy.
Fix it on the router: turn on Smart Queue, SQM or Adaptive QoS (names vary), set to about 90% of your measured speed.
No such setting on your router? Pause Steam, console and Windows downloads while you play.
Changing DNS doesn't change in-game ping. DNS only looks up addresses before you connect.
'Ping booster' apps and registry network tweaks can't make packets travel faster. Most games don't even use the settings they change.
Turning off IPv6 doesn't help, and can break some connections.

Guides.Title: Temperatures, dust and fan noise
Guides.Summary: Which temperatures are fine, how to stop heat slowing your games down, and how to make a PC quieter.

Steps.Text: Graphics card while gaming: 60 to 80 °C is normal. Its hot spot runs 10 to 20 °C higher.
CPU while gaming: up to the high 80s °C is fine on modern chips. Many are designed to boost until they reach about 90 to 95 °C.
A problem looks like this: FPS drops after 10 to 20 minutes while temperatures sit at their limit and clocks fall.
Clean the dust: PC off and unplugged, short bursts of compressed air, hold fans still so they don't spin. Front filters first.
Airflow: front fans pull air in, rear and top fans push it out. A little more in than out keeps dust down.
Undervolt the graphics card: often 10 °C cooler at the same FPS. On NVIDIA, Pulse's GPU tuning page walks you through it.
Still hot after three or more years? Fresh thermal paste on the CPU cooler usually helps. On a graphics card it can affect the warranty, so check first.
Laptops: hard flat surface, back raised a little, vents clean, and the maker's performance mode while plugged in.
Set gentle fan curves in the BIOS (usually under Hardware Monitor or Smart Fan).
Cap your FPS. A card rendering 300 FPS in a menu is working, and spinning its fans, for nothing.
